04.01.title: Error analysis and convergence order
04.01.html:
Every numerical method trades effort for accuracy. The question an engineer asks is not “is it accurate?” but “how fast does the error fall when I pay more?” That rate, the order of convergence, is the single most useful number for comparing methods, choosing step sizes and catching bugs. A solver that should be second order but measures as first order has a mistake in it, every time.

Two kinds of convergence

Iterative methods (root finders, linear solvers) produce a sequence x0​,x1​,… with error en​=∣xn​−x∗∣. The method has order p if

en+1​≈Cenp​.

p=1 is linear (each step multiplies the error by C<1), p=2 is quadratic (the number of correct digits roughly doubles per step).

Discretisation methods (finite differences, quadrature, ODE solvers) have a step h and error

E(h)≈Khp.

Halving h divides the error by 2p: by 4 for a second-order method, by 16 for a fourth-order one.

Measuring the order from data

Take logs and the power law becomes a straight line. For an iteration, three consecutive errors give

p≈ln(en​/en−1​)ln(en+1​/en​)​.

For a discretisation, two step sizes give p≈ln(E1​/E2​)/ln(h1​/h2​); with more points, fit a line to logE against logh. When the exact answer is unknown, compare three solutions at h, h/2, h/4: p≈log2​((uh​−uh/2​)/(uh/2​−uh/4​)).

Truncation versus round-off

Shrinking h reduces the truncation error Khp, but every function value carries a relative rounding error near ε≈2.2×10−16, and a difference formula divides it by h. The total error behaves like

E(h)≈Khp+hε∣f∣​,

so there is a best step. For the forward difference (p=1) it’s near ε​≈10−8; for the central difference (p=2) near ε1/3≈6×10−6. Below that, the error grows again.

Worked exampleNewton’s order, measured

Solve Wallis’s cubic x3−2x−5=0 (root x∗=2.0945515) with Newton’s method from x0​=3.

  1. Errors: 0.91, 0.27, 3.3×10−2, 5.8×10−4, 1.9×10−7, 2.1×10−14.
  2. Last triple: p≈ln(2.1×10−14/1.9×10−7)/ln(1.9×10−7/5.8×10−4)=2.00.
  3. Theory predicts C=∣f′′(x∗)/(2f′(x∗))∣=6x∗/(2(3x∗2−2))=0.563. Check: 2.1×10−14/(1.9×10−7)2≈0.58.
  4. The secant method on the same equation measures p≈1.61, close to the golden ratio 1.618 that theory predicts.

Exercise 1Read the order off a table

A solver for a beam deflection returns u=4.2860 mm at h=0.1 m, 4.2884 mm at h=0.05 m and 4.2890 mm at h=0.025 m. What order does it show, and what is the extrapolated answer?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Differences: 4.2884−4.2860=0.0024 and 4.2890−4.2884=0.0006.
  2. Ratio 0.0024/0.0006=4, so p=log2​4=2: second order.
  3. Richardson extrapolation: u≈uh/4​+(uh/4​−uh/2​)/(2p−1)=4.2890+0.0006/3=4.2892 mm.

quiz.explain: 0.5×10−6=5×10−7.

quiz.explain: ln(10−1.5)/ln(10−1)=1.5.

quiz.explain: 24.

quiz.explain: Rounding errors of size ε are divided by h.

quiz.explain: 6x∗/(2(3x∗2−2)).

04.02.title: Root finding toolbox
04.02.html:
Engineering is full of equations you cannot rearrange: the Colebrook friction factor in a pipe, the natural frequencies of a beam, the operating point of a pump on a system curve. You met bisection and Newton in Phase 01. This lesson builds the toolbox a professional uses: know which method is safe, which is fast, and how to combine them so you get both.

The trade-off

Method Needs Order Can fail?
Bisection a bracket [a,b] with a sign change 1 (halves the bracket) no
Newton f′ and a good start 2 yes: diverges, cycles, f′=0
Secant two starting points 1.618 yes
Brent a bracket superlinear no

Bisection is guaranteed but slow: to shrink a bracket of width L to δ takes ⌈log2​(L/δ)⌉ steps, independent of the function. Newton is fast but needs a derivative and can be thrown far away by a flat region.

Secant: Newton without the derivative

Replace f′(xn​) by the slope through the last two points:

xn+1​=xn​−f(xn​)f(xn​)−f(xn−1​)xn​−xn−1​​.

One new function evaluation per step and order φ=1.618. Per evaluation that beats Newton (which needs f and f′) whenever the derivative costs more than about 44% of a function call.

Brent: fast when it can be, safe when it must be

Brent’s method keeps a bracket at all times. Each step it tries a fast interpolation step: inverse quadratic interpolation through the last three points (fit x as a quadratic in y and set y=0), or a secant step. It accepts that step only if it lands inside the bracket and shrinks the interval well enough; otherwise it bisects. So it is never slower than bisection by more than a constant factor and usually converges superlinearly. It’s what scipy.optimize.brentq runs.

Worked exampleFriction factor in a water main

Find the Darcy friction factor f for Re=105 and relative roughness ε/D=10−4 from Colebrook:

f​1​=−2log10​(3.7ε/D​+Ref​2.51​).
  1. Solve for x=1/f​: g(x)=x+2log10​(ε/D/3.7+2.51x/Re)=0.
  2. Bracket: g(1)=−7.57 and g(20)=+13.45, so a root lies in [1,20].
  3. Brent converges in 6 iterations to x=7.3494, so f=1/x2=0.01851. Bisection needs 45 iterations for the same 10−12 tolerance.
  4. Sanity check against the explicit Swamee-Jain approximation: 0.01845, within 0.4%.

Exercise 1Choose the method

You need the first natural frequency of a clamped beam from cosβcoshβ=−1, inside a design loop that calls it 10 000 times. The derivative is easy. Which method do you use and how do you start it?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The root near β=1.875 lies in the bracket [1,3]: cos1cosh1+1=1.83>0 and cos3cosh3+1=−8.97<0.
  2. Brent with that bracket is safe and fast. Newton is faster per step, but coshβ grows quickly, so a bad start can throw it to another root.
  3. A good compromise for the loop: Newton started from the previous design’s root, falling back to Brent if a step leaves the bracket. That is the same idea Brent uses internally.

04.03.title: Nonlinear systems
04.03.html:
Real structures rarely give you one equation in one unknown. A cable net, a linkage, a pipe network or a large-deflection frame gives you n coupled nonlinear equations F(x)=0. Newton’s method carries over almost unchanged: replace the derivative by the Jacobian matrix and the division by a linear solve. It is the engine inside every nonlinear finite-element code.

Newton in n dimensions

Linearise around the current guess:

F(x+Δx)≈F(x)+J(x)Δx,Jij​=∂xj​∂Fi​​.

Set the linear model to zero and solve for the step:

J(xk​)Δx=−F(xk​),xk+1​=xk​+Δx.

Never invert J; solve the system (LU from Phase 02). Near the solution the convergence is quadratic: the residual norm squares each step.

Where the Jacobian comes from

  • By hand, when the equations are simple. Best accuracy and speed.
  • By finite differences, column by column: J:,j​≈(F(x+hej​)−F(x−hej​))/(2h). Costs 2n residual evaluations. Always use it to check a hand-derived Jacobian.
  • By automatic differentiation, in modern frameworks.

A node held by two cables

A node at p hangs from elastic cables anchored at ai​ with unstretched length L0,i​ and axial stiffness EA. With di​=ai​−p, Li​=∣di​∣ and ui​=di​/Li​, each cable pulls with tension Ti​=L0,i​EA​(Li​−L0,i​) (zero if slack). Equilibrium is

F(p)=i∑​Ti​ui​+(0−W​)=0.

Differentiating gives the tangent stiffness, two physical parts per cable:

J=−i∑​[ki​ui​uiT​+Li​Ti​​(I−ui​uiT​)],ki​=L0,i​EA​.

The first term is the cable’s axial stiffness. The second is the geometric stiffness: a taut cable resists sideways motion in proportion to its tension, which is why a guitar string gets stiffer as you tune it up.

Worked exampleEquilibrium of the two-cable node

Anchors at (0,0) and (4,0) m, L0​=2.5 m and 2.0 m, EA=50 kN, W=2000 N, start at (2,−2) m.

  1. At the start both cables are 2.828 m long, so both are stretched; residual norm 2.0×104 N.
  2. Newton residuals: 2.0×104→2.9×103→2.6×102→3.2→6.4×10−4→2.7×10−11 N. Five steps, quadratic at the end.
  3. Solution p=(2.2991,−1.1971) m. Cable lengths 2.5921 m and 2.0799 m.
  4. Tensions T1​=50000⋅0.0921/2.5=1842 N and T2​=50000⋅0.0799/2.0=1997 N. Their vertical components add up to W.

Exercise 1One Newton step by hand

Solve x2+y2=4, xy=1 starting from (x,y)=(2,0.5). Take one Newton step and compare with the exact root in that quadrant.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. F=(x2+y2−4, xy−1)=(0.25, 0) and J=(2xy​2yx​)=(40.5​12​), detJ=7.5.
  2. Δ=−J−1F=−7.51​(2−0.5​−14​)(0.250​)=(−0.0667, 0.0167).
  3. New point (1.9333, 0.5167).
  4. Exact: x2+1/x2=4 gives x2=2+3​, so x=1.9319, y=0.5176. One step already has three correct digits.

04.04.title: Interpolation
04.04.html:
Measurements and tables give you values at a few points: a thermocouple calibration, a steam table, a cam profile, a wind-tunnel sweep. Interpolation fills in between. The obvious idea, one polynomial through all the points, works beautifully for a handful of points and fails spectacularly for many equally spaced ones. Understanding why tells you where to put your sample points.

Lagrange form

Through n+1 points (xj​,yj​) there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n:

p(x)=j=0∑n​yj​ℓj​(x),ℓj​(x)=k=j∏​xj​−xk​x−xk​​.

Each basis polynomial ℓj​ is 1 at its own node and 0 at the others. For computing, use the barycentric form, which is stable and costs O(n) per evaluation:

p(x)=∑j​x−xj​wj​​∑j​x−xj​wj​​yj​​,wj​=∏k=j​(xj​−xk​)1​.

The error formula and Runge’s phenomenon

For a smooth f,

f(x)−p(x)=(n+1)!f(n+1)(ξ)​j=0∏n​(x−xj​).

Two factors fight: the derivative term and the node polynomial ∏(x−xj​). For equally spaced nodes the node polynomial is tiny in the middle and huge near the ends. For f=1/(1+25x2) on [−1,1], the derivatives grow fast enough that the error near the ends grows with n: Runge’s phenomenon.

Chebyshev nodes

Choose nodes that cluster towards the ends:

xk​=cos2(n+1)(2k+1)π​,k=0,…,n.

They make max∣∏(x−xk​)∣=2−n, the smallest possible, and for any smooth function the interpolation error then falls as n grows. When you can choose where to measure, measure at Chebyshev points.

Worked exampleThermocouple between table values

A type K thermocouple gives 0 mV at 0 °C, 4.096 mV at 100 °C and 8.138 mV at 200 °C. Estimate the voltage at 150 °C.

  1. ℓ0​(150)=(0−100)(0−200)(150−100)(150−200)​=−0.125.
  2. ℓ1​(150)=(100−0)(100−200)(150−0)(150−200)​=0.75, and ℓ2​(150)=200⋅100150⋅50​=0.375.
  3. p(150)=0+0.75⋅4.096+0.375⋅8.138=6.124 mV.
  4. The reference table gives 6.138 mV. The 0.014 mV gap is about 0.35 °C at roughly 41 µV/°C: fine for a quick check, not for calibration, where you’d use more points or a spline.

The script prints, for Runge’s function:

n equispaced max error Chebyshev max error
5 0.433 0.556
10 1.916 0.109
15 2.108 0.083
20 59.8 0.015

At very low degree Chebyshev is not automatically better, but only Chebyshev keeps improving.

Exercise 1Why not just use more points?

A colleague fits a degree-20 polynomial through 21 equally spaced points of a measured cam lift curve and finds wild oscillations near the ends. Give two fixes.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Measure at Chebyshev-spaced angles instead, if the rig allows it. The node polynomial is then evenly small across the interval.
  2. Use piecewise interpolation: a cubic spline (next lesson) through the same 21 points. Each piece only sees its neighbours, so the error is controlled locally and doesn’t grow with the number of points.
  3. If the data are noisy, don’t interpolate at all: fit a low-degree least-squares model (Phase 02) or a smoothing spline.

04.05.title: Splines
04.05.html:
A draughtsman bending a thin wooden strip through pins on a drawing board was solving a variational problem: the strip settles into the shape with the least bending energy. That shape, piecewise cubic with continuous slope and curvature, is the cubic spline. It’s how CAD tools draw smooth curves, how cam profiles are designed and how you interpolate measured data without Runge’s wiggles.

Conditions on each piece

Between knots xi​ and xi+1​ (spacing hi​) the spline is a cubic Si​(x). With n intervals there are 4n coefficients. Conditions:

  • Si​(xi​)=yi​ and Si​(xi+1​)=yi+1​: 2n conditions.
  • slope continuous at the n−1 interior knots.
  • second derivative (curvature) continuous at the interior knots.

That is 4n−2. The last two come from the ends: a natural spline sets S′′=0 at both ends (a free strip), a clamped spline prescribes the end slopes.

Solve for the curvatures

Use the knot second derivatives Mi​=S′′(xi​) as unknowns. Within an interval S′′ is linear, so integrating twice and imposing the values gives, with A=(xi+1​−x)/hi​ and B=1−A,

S(x)=Ayi​+Byi+1​+6hi2​​[(A3−A)Mi​+(B3−B)Mi+1​].

Slope continuity at each interior knot then becomes one equation linking three neighbours:

hi−1​Mi−1​+2(hi−1​+hi​)Mi​+hi​Mi+1​=6(hi​yi+1​−yi​​−hi−1​yi​−yi−1​​).

The matrix is tridiagonal and diagonally dominant, so the Thomas algorithm (Gaussian elimination without fill-in) solves it in O(n) operations. A million-knot spline costs milliseconds.

Worked exampleA four-knot natural spline by hand

Knots (0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1), all h=1, natural ends M0​=M3​=0.

  1. Knot 1: M0​+4M1​+M2​=6(y0​−2y1​+y2​)=−12.
  2. Knot 2: M1​+4M2​+M3​=6(y1​−2y2​+y3​)=12.
  3. Solve 4M1​+M2​=−12, M1​+4M2​=12: M1​=−4, M2​=4.
  4. At x=0.5 (A=B=0.5): S=0.5⋅0+0.5⋅1+61​(−0.375⋅0−0.375⋅(−4))=0.5+0.25=0.75.

The continuity test is worth having: an early version of the code above built the sub-diagonal from the wrong spacings. With uneven knots the curve still passed through every point and looked fine, but the slope jumped at the third station. Only the test caught it.

Exercise 1Natural or clamped?

A cam profile must start from rest: lift 0 and slope 0 at θ=0. Which end condition do you use there, and what does a natural spline do instead?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Use a clamped end with S′(0)=0, so the follower velocity starts at zero.
  2. A natural spline forces S′′(0)=0 instead and leaves the slope free; the follower would start with a nonzero velocity, a velocity jump and an infinite acceleration spike at the start.
  3. For cams you often need continuous jerk too, which leads to quintic splines or B-splines of higher degree.

04.06.title: Numerical differentiation of noisy data
04.06.html:
A displacement sensor on a test rig gives you position every millisecond. You want velocity and acceleration. Differentiating the samples directly, with the finite differences from Phase 01, produces garbage: each difference divides a small noise by a small step. This lesson quantifies the problem and fixes it the way instrumentation engineers do, by fitting before differentiating.

Why noise explodes

Write each sample as xi​=x(ti​)+ηi​ with independent noise of standard deviation σ. The central difference gives

2hxi+1​−xi−1​​=x′(ti​)+truncation6h2​x′′′​​+noise2hηi+1​−ηi−1​​​​.

The noise term has standard deviation 2​σ/(2h)=σ/(2​h). Sampling faster makes it worse. A second derivative is worse again, scaling like σ/h2. At 1 kHz with 0.1 mm noise the velocity noise is about 0.07 m/s, and a raw second difference has about 245 m/s² of noise, 25 g.

Fit first: Savitzky-Golay

Around each sample take a window of 2m+1 points, fit a low-degree polynomial by least squares (Phase 02), and differentiate the polynomial at the centre. Because the fit is linear in the data, the whole operation is a fixed set of weights ck​, a convolution:

x^′(ti​)=k=−m∑m​ck​xi+k​.

For a quadratic (or linear) fit the first-derivative weights are simply ck​=k/(h∑k2), the least-squares slope. Their noise gain is σ/(h∑k2​), which falls like m−3/2. The price is bias: a wide window flattens fast features. Choose the window to span a small fraction of the shortest period you care about.

Worked exampleVelocity from a shaker test

Position x=0.05sin(2π⋅1.5t) m, sampled at h=1 ms with σ=0.1 mm noise. True peak speed 0.05⋅2π⋅1.5=0.471 m/s.

  1. Raw central difference: predicted noise σ/(2​h)=10−4/(1.414×10−3)=0.0707 m/s; measured RMS error 0.0718 m/s, 15% of the peak.
  2. Savitzky-Golay, 51-point window, quadratic: noise gain σ/(h2∑125​k2​)=10−4/(10−3⋅105.1)=0.00095 m/s.
  3. Measured RMS error 0.00213 m/s, which includes the small bias of fitting a parabola over 51 ms of a 667 ms period. Better than raw by a factor of 34.

Exercise 1Acceleration from the same data

Estimate the noise in a raw second difference (xi+1​−2xi​+xi−1​)/h2 for σ=0.1 mm and h=1 ms, and compare with the true peak acceleration.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The noise is (ηi+1​−2ηi​+ηi−1​)/h2, with variance (1+4+1)σ2/h4, so standard deviation 6​σ/h2=2.449⋅10−4/10−6=245 m/s².
  2. True peak acceleration 0.05(2π⋅1.5)2=4.44 m/s².
  3. The noise is 55 times the signal. You must smooth (a Savitzky-Golay second-derivative filter or a low-pass filter) or measure acceleration directly with an accelerometer.

04.07.title: Gaussian quadrature
04.07.html:
Every finite-element stiffness matrix, every mass matrix and every load vector is built from integrals over elements, evaluated millions of times. Each function evaluation costs. Gaussian quadrature answers a sharp question: with n evaluations, what is the most accurate rule possible? Answer: place the points at the roots of a Legendre polynomial and you integrate every polynomial up to degree 2n−1 exactly, twice what equally spaced points achieve.

Counting the freedom

A rule ∫−11​f(x)dx≈∑i=1n​wi​f(xi​) has 2n free numbers: n nodes and n weights. Demanding exactness for 1,x,x2,…,x2n−1 gives 2n equations. For n=2, symmetry gives x1,2​=±a, w1​=w2​=1 (from ∫1=2), and ∫x2=2/3 requires 2a2=2/3:

∫−11​fdx≈f(−3​1​)+f(3​1​),

exact for cubics. The three-point rule uses 0 and ±3/5​ with weights 8/9 and 5/9.

Why Legendre roots

Divide a polynomial f of degree ≤2n−1 by the Legendre polynomial Pn​: f=qPn​+r with q and r of degree ≤n−1. Legendre polynomials are orthogonal, so ∫qPn​=0. At the roots of Pn​, f(xi​)=r(xi​), and an n-point rule with the right weights is exact for the degree-(n−1) remainder r. So the rule is exact for f.

Computing nodes: Golub-Welsch

Legendre polynomials satisfy a three-term recurrence, which can be written as an eigenvalue problem. The nodes are the eigenvalues of the symmetric tridiagonal matrix with off-diagonal entries βk​=k/4k2−1​, and the weights are wi​=2v1,i2​ from the first components of the normalised eigenvectors. Phase 02’s eigenvalue machinery does the rest.

For an interval [a,b], map x=2b−a​t+2a+b​ and multiply the sum by 2b−a​.

Worked exampleTwo points, exact cubic

Integrate f(x)=x3+x2 on [0,2] with the two-point rule.

  1. Map: x=t+1, scale factor (b−a)/2=1. Nodes x=1∓0.57735: 0.42265 and 1.57735.
  2. f(0.42265)=0.25413 and f(1.57735)=6.41253.
  3. Sum: 6.66667. Exact: 424​+323​=4+2.66667=6.66667. Exact, as promised for a cubic.
  4. For ∫02​e−x2dx=0.882081, errors with 2 to 6 points are 3.7×10−2, 3.2×10−3, 1.5×10−4, 3.4×10−6, 3.5×10−8. Simpson with 5 points is still at 2.7×10−4.

Exercise 1How many points for an element?

A 2D bilinear quadrilateral element with a constant material has a stiffness integrand that, on a rectangular element, is a polynomial of degree 2 in each direction. How many Gauss points per direction integrate it exactly, and how many in total?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. n points are exact to degree 2n−1. Degree 2 needs 2n−1≥2, so n=2.
  2. Use a tensor product: 2×2=4 points per element. That is the standard “full integration” of a bilinear quad.
  3. Using only 1 point (“reduced integration”) is cheaper and avoids shear locking in bending, but it can admit zero-energy hourglass modes. Phase 16 (finite elements) comes back to this.

04.08.title: Explicit Euler and stability
04.08.html:
A simulation that runs for a while and then shoots off to 10300 is the most common surprise in engineering computing. It is rarely a bug in the physics. It is the time step violating the stability limit of the integrator. You can predict that limit exactly with one line of algebra, and this lesson shows how.

The test equation

Linearise any system around an operating point and diagonalise it: each mode behaves like

y′=λy,y(0)=1,y(t)=eλt,

with λ an eigenvalue of the Jacobian (Phase 02). Real negative λ is a decaying mode (cooling, damping); complex λ with negative real part is a damped oscillation.

One step of Euler

Explicit Euler, yn+1​=yn​+hf(yn​), applied to the test equation gives

yn+1​=(1+hλ)yn​⟹yn​=(1+hλ)n.

The numerical solution decays only if the amplification factor satisfies ∣1+hλ∣≤1. In the complex z=hλ plane that is a disc of radius 1 centred at −1: the stability region. For a real decay rate λ=−k:

∣1−hk∣≤1⟺h≤k2​.

For 1/k<h<2/k the solution still decays but flips sign every step: stable, but qualitatively wrong. Purely imaginary λ (an undamped oscillator) is never inside the disc: Euler always adds energy to a spring-mass system.

Stiffness

For a system, every mode must be stable, so the fastest mode sets the step, even after it has decayed to nothing. Eigenvalues −1 and −1000 force h<0.002 s, so 5000 steps to cover 10 s of a slow transient. That is a stiff system, and lesson 04.11 cures it with implicit methods.

Worked exampleA thermocouple bead

A bead with time constant τ=0.5 s obeys y′=−2y (k=2 s⁻¹). Integrate with explicit Euler for 50 steps.

h (s) 1−hk size after 50 steps
0.1 0.8 1.4×10−5
0.5 0 0 (one step lands on the answer)
0.9 −0.8 1.4×10−5, sign flipping
1.0 −1 1, oscillating forever
1.1 −1.2 9.1×103, blown up

The boundary is exactly h=2/k=1 s, and the code checks it at 59 step sizes.

Exercise 1Step limit for a damped oscillator

A suspension mode has λ=−0.5±3i s⁻¹. What is the largest stable explicit Euler step?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Need ∣1+hλ∣2=(1−0.5h)2+(3h)2≤1.
  2. Expand: 1−h+0.25h2+9h2≤1, so h(9.25h−1)≤0.
  3. h≤1/9.25=0.108 s. In general h≤−2Reλ/∣λ∣2: lightly damped oscillators need tiny steps.

04.09.title: Runge-Kutta methods
04.09.html:
Euler’s method looks at the slope once per step and walks in a straight line. Runge-Kutta methods sample the slope several times inside the step and combine the samples so that the errors cancel up to a high power of h. Classical RK4 needs four slope evaluations per step and is fourth order: halve the step and the error drops 16 times. It’s been the workhorse for well-behaved ODEs for over a century.

Deriving RK2 by matching Taylor series

Propose a two-stage method for y′=f(t,y):

k1​=f(tn​,yn​),k2​=f(tn​+c2​h, yn​+a21​hk1​),yn+1​=yn​+h(b1​k1​+b2​k2​).

Expand k2​ to first order: k2​≈f+c2​hft​+a21​hffy​. The exact solution has y(t+h)=y+hf+2h2​(ft​+ffy​)+O(h3). Matching terms:

b1​+b2​=1,b2​c2​=21​,b2​a21​=21​.

One free parameter. b2​=21​ gives Heun’s method (c2​=1); b2​=1 gives the midpoint method (c2​=21​). Both have local error O(h3) and global error O(h2).

Butcher tableaus

Any explicit RK method is a table of coefficients: ci​ (stage times), aij​ (how stages combine) and bi​ (final weights). Classical RK4:

021​21​1​21​0061​​21​031​​131​​61​​​

One engine that reads a tableau can run every method, which is how libraries are written. The code below does exactly that.

Is more stages always better?

Cost is counted in function evaluations. To reach error 10−6 on a smooth problem, RK4 typically needs far fewer evaluations than Euler: in the example below, RK4 with 200 evaluations beats Euler with 20 000 by more than two orders of magnitude. For non-smooth problems (impacts, friction switching) the high order is wasted at the discontinuities, which is one reason adaptive methods (next lesson) exist.

Worked exampleMeasured orders on a pendulum

θ¨=−(g/L)sinθ, L=1 m, θ0​=60°, integrated to t=2 s. Reference angle 54.367907° (also confirmed with SciPy at tolerance 10−12). Error in radians:

method n=50 n=100 observed order
Euler 2.6×10−1 1.4×10−1 0.98
Heun 5.6×10−3 1.3×10−3 2.07
midpoint 6.1×10−3 1.4×10−3 2.06
RK4 4.4×10−6 2.5×10−7 4.08

The order is measured from n=100 and n=200.

Exercise 1Ralston’s method

Choose b2​=43​ in the RK2 family. Find b1​, c2​ and a21​, and write the method.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. b1​=1−b2​=41​.
  2. c2​=a21​=2b2​1​=32​.
  3. k1​=f(tn​,yn​), k2​=f(tn​+32​h, yn​+32​hk1​), yn+1​=yn​+4h​(k1​+3k2​). This is Ralston’s method, the RK2 choice with the smallest error constant.

04.10.title: Adaptive step size
04.10.html:
A ball dropped on a hard floor spends almost a second in smooth free flight and under two milliseconds in contact, where the forces are thousands of times larger. A fixed step small enough for the contact wastes thousands of steps in flight; a step sized for the flight jumps straight through the floor. Adaptive integrators measure their own error every step and adjust h to meet a tolerance you set. They’re the default in every serious ODE library.

Estimating the error for free

Run two methods of different order from the same point and compare. An embedded pair shares all its stage evaluations: the Dormand-Prince pair computes seven stages, combines them one way for a fifth-order result y(5) and another way for a fourth-order y(4). Their difference estimates the local error of the lower-order one:

err=​atol+rtol∣y∣y(5)−y(4)​​RMS​.

Scaling by atol+rtol∣y∣ makes err≤1 mean “within tolerance”. The method then carries on with the fifth-order value (local extrapolation), and since the seventh stage equals the first stage of the next step, each accepted step costs six new evaluations.

Choosing the next step

Local error of a fourth-order estimate scales like h5, so to hit err=1:

hnew​=h⋅min(5, max(0.2, 0.9err−1/5)).

If err>1 the step is rejected and retried with the smaller h. The safety factor 0.9 and the limits 0.2 and 5 stop the controller from oscillating.

Local tolerance, global error

The controller bounds the error made in each step, not the accumulated error at the end. For well-behaved problems the global error ends up close to the tolerance, which the code checks; for chaotic or unstable problems it can be much larger. Always repeat a run at a tighter tolerance and compare: if the answer changes, it wasn’t converged.

Large steps also mean the solution is only known at a few points. To plot it, or to find the apex of a bounce, use dense output: an interpolant built from the stage values. The widget below uses a cubic Hermite curve through the position and velocity at each accepted step, which is exact for a free-flight parabola.

Worked exampleTolerance versus accuracy, and a bouncing ball

  1. Harmonic oscillator y′′=−y, y(0)=1, to t=10 (exact cos10):
rtol steps global error
10−4 23 1.5×10−4
10−6 53 1.2×10−6
10−8 129 1.1×10−8

Each factor of 100 in tolerance costs about 1001/5≈2.5 times more steps, as a fifth-order method should.

  1. Ball, m=0.06 kg, contact stiffness 2×105 N/m, damping 8 N s/m, rtol 10−6: 47 steps for the first second. Largest step in flight 390 ms, smallest in contact 3.6 µs, a ratio of about 105.
  2. Physics check: contact time πm/k​=1.72 ms; damping ratio ζ=8/(22×105⋅0.06​)=0.0365, so restitution e=e−ζπ/1−ζ2​=0.892 and rebound height e2×1 m =0.795 m. The solver gives 0.795 m.
